conclusion: The base provider took 146% of wire time per snapshot step, above the 110% target and the 109% model figure at 200 ns per access; the register accesses and provider software around them explain the 287 us. The provider follow-up in pmic-access.md reduced the step to 779 to 796 us, still above 110%, so the 110% target is replaced by the provisional empirical bound.
narrative:
34 steps: two supply-verification snapshots, then 32 client snapshots of DCDC2 and DCDC4 in turn. Percentages are relative to the 630 us bit-time wire time; the model's own bytes take 23 us, so its earlier 107% is relative to 642 us.
| Metric | Board | Model, 200 ns per access | Model, 1,300 ns per access |
| Snapshot step | 917 us (22,019 ticks median); 916 to 924 us in steps 2 to 34; 941 us in step 1 | 687 us | 915 us |
| Against 630 us | 146% (median); 149.4% in step 1 | 109% | 145% |
| Steps and tick waits per snapshot | 1 and 0 | 1 and 0 | 1 and 0 |

The 287 us per step beyond wire time divide as follows. Tick interrupts: none measurable. Thirty of steps 2 to 34 held one scheduler tick and three held none; medians 22,019 and 22,025 ticks differ by 0.25 us, and the steps with a tick span 916 to 919 us. Service polling: one extra read per phase and no extra rounds. In steps 2 to 34 each of the 36 phases that wait for the interrupt flag (12 conditions and 24 bytes) read the control register exactly twice, the first right after the phase starts (flag clear) and the second after the spin (flag set); in step 1 one phase found the flag set at its first read. The spin never ended before the controller did, and the service never polled a phase a third time. Register accesses account for nearly all of it: a snapshot makes 211 accesses (151 reads, 60 writes) in the host model; the board's 3,095 control-register reads, 91 per step, match the model's count. The host model reproduces the board median at 1,300 ns per access instead of 200 ns.

The 1,300 ns is a fit; the run did not measure how it divides. It covers the bus access with its two DSB SY and the provider's software around each access. The disassembled read path of the bundle 6 image is about 220 instructions: two deadline reads, each with an ISB and a 64-bit division of the counter; a task check that masks IRQs and calls two FreeRTOS functions; the address allowlist; and bundle 6's TWI observer. The owner's reads in the same run, using a leaner accessor with the bundle's recording, are 0.42 to 1.17 us apart: 0.42 to 0.54 us between CCU reads and 0.63 to 0.96 us (median 0.71 us) between consecutive reads of R_CCU and the PPU block, in the 0x07000000 region that also holds S_TWI0. An estimated half of the fitted cost is provider software, which performance-architecture.md section 1.1 and items 4 and 5 of section 2 prescribe removing (one deadline check per bus phase instead of two per access; ownership checked once at enter() with the per-access revocation load kept). Production images have no TWI observer, so their accesses cost less than the fitted figure.

The accesses lengthen the step because of where the service starts each spin: pmic() starts each phase's spin from a time read made after the poll that started the phase has returned, so the accesses of that poll after the phase-start write and of the next poll before its phase-start write add to the wire time. The follow-up (pmic-access.md) times each spin from the provider's time of the phase-start write with a minimum re-spin of a quarter bit time and reads the time once per bus phase.

Follow-up runs (bundle 6, port 3-3, 2026-10-24, CPU-L 494 MHz, trace observer and write stamps active): median steps 779 us and 784 us (123.7% and 124.4% of 630 us), first steps 809 us and 807 us; bytes 22.5 us and 22.541 us; no re-spin. Timed in the service task: bare S_TWI0 read about 378 ns, DSB SY pair adds about 41 ns, adapter read 462 ns, time read 144 ns, fenced write in a transfer about 360 ns with its stamp, plain write 198 ns, whole provider poll that finds the flag clear 1,176 ns. At those costs the model gives 739 us; the 45 us it lacks corresponds to about 1 us in each of the 42 phases. A third run timed each completing poll: median 796.4 us with that window; byte polls 3.10 us against the model's 2.72 us; the completing polls account for about 12 us of the per-step difference and about 38 us lies in step work outside them (admission lock waits, publication). The 110% target (693 us) is out of reach of a provider that polls each bus phase: charging the register accesses alone the model gives 712 us with DSB SY pairs and 694 us with plain reads, a plain DATA write and a DSB SY after the CNTR write. That lighter placement was qualified for snapshots by a bundle 6 run and shortened that run's median by 1.9 us. A route to 110% needs fewer serial accesses per snapshot, such as the S_TWI0 packet engine; neither it nor a Device-nGnRE mapping of S_TWI0 is designed.

Provisional bound: at 400 kHz a snapshot completes in one step; median limit 1,268 permille of the measured wire time; first-step limit adds 40 us (798.840 us and 838.840 us at nominal 22.5 us bytes, approximately 799 us and 839 us). They come from the first follow-up run's median plus approximately 20 us and hold for bundle 6 at CPU-L 494 MHz on one service core with its trace observer and write stamps. The second run applied them and passed. At a step near 1 ms the service can split a snapshot across a tick wait. The DCDC3 selector-write bound is at most two steps with one tick wait, pending a board run; at the measured costs the model writes the selector in one 950 us step, and at the poll cost fitted to the board median it splits the write into two steps with one tick wait.

narrative:
Merge base / now:
- Tick waits per snapshot; per selector write: 44 and 56 polls, up to one tick each -> model at 200 ns per register access, 400 kHz: 0 and 0, one step of 687 us and 885 us (wire time 642 us and 828 us, so 107%). Model at the board's fitted 1,300 ns: snapshot 0, one step of 915 us (145% of 630 us); selector write 1, in 2 steps. Board snapshot: one step of 917 us, 146% (median of 34); with the provider follow-up 779 us, 123.7% (median of 33). 100 kHz model: 2 and 3, at most 1,000 us spin per step.
- BUSY results seen by another caller during one snapshot: a733_pmic_live 211 per snapshot -> a733_pmic_live 0; a733_pmic_result at most 1 with two cores, 0 with one; a733_pmic_reap 0.
- CPU time USB0 waits behind the service: PMIC task at or above USB0 priority in all five images -> 0: the service runs below USB0 in all five images, the owner's code has no critical section or scheduler suspension, and the provider's lock waits at activation are one-tick blocks that USB0 preempts.
- Service wakes per second with no work: 1,000 -> 0; 2 in the resident board image, which caps the block at 500 ms; one wake per park, stop or row notification.
- Row-state read by GPU platform poll, framebuffer and G2D: DE_SYS poll while waiting 344 instructions, a lock entry and 2 register reads -> 12 instructions, 1 acquire load, no exclusive access.
- Ticks from row request to visible ON, acknowledgement within 50 us: DE_SYS 1, GPU 0 -> 1 for the GPU and the framebuffer at their next poll; G2D reads the same row the same way.
- PMIC result polls by the other submitters: one per tick -> one per tick. PMIC transactions per row request: GPU 6 per start (one DCDC4 snapshot) -> 0; 12 per boot.
- Slow acknowledgement: DE_SYS one caller poll per tick; GPU a 50 us spin per poll -> 54 us spin after the command, then one status read per one-tick step; FAILED 10,092 us after the command, after 10 retries.
- Register accesses per domain-5 ON: 13 PPU operations by the GPU (14 with the native read-modify-write of the policy word) -> 14 PPU accesses by the owner (2 adoption reads, 5 delay-row writes and 5 readbacks, the command, 1 status read), plus 5 domain-level reads.
- Files that write the delay row: 6 plus 2 native allowlists -> 4 with no native allowlist before the GPU controller wrote domain 6; 5 with the GPU native allowlist after.
- Supply verification ends 8.4 ms after the service's first step at 400 kHz and 15.0 ms at 100 kHz (flags at sub-microsecond times, model); model supply verification after the first step: see pmic-access host budgets (8,383 us; 15,010 us).

At 400 kHz and 200 ns per register access each request takes one step of 107% of the model wire time: the step adds polls and time reads to the bus phases. Baseline counts at the design commit b3b1289 were taken with the budget-table host models. Design budget table (baseline -> target, measured by): tick waits 44 and 56 polls -> 400 kHz snapshot 0 / one step; BUSY of a733_pmic_live whenever it meets a poll -> 0; USB0 behind service: PMIC task at or above USB0 in every image -> 0; service wakes 1,000 -> 0; row-state read: platform register lock and 2 reads per poll -> <= 100 instructions; ticks to ON: DE_SYS >= 1, GPU 0 -> 1; PMIC transactions per row request GPU 6 per start -> 0, 12 per boot; slow acknowledgement one caller poll per tick -> <= 1 tick per retry; register accesses per domain-5 ON 14 counted from the GPU steps -> 14; files writing the delay row 6 plus 2 native allowlists -> 5 with one native allowlist (new checks/power-domains-tree.py). The service check also covers the park paths: a park request in the GPU display image completes only when the PMIC is idle and every domain is ON, OFF or FAILED with no row transition pending; the GPU finite-return stop and the GPU liveness park complete before their deadlines.

hypothesis: The owner enforces a strict 10 ms transition deadline and keeps the accelerator OFF/ON lifecycle contract of the GPU and NPU.
prediction: A status observation at or after the deadline is rejected; a failed or regressed completion clock fails the service and every pending domain; an expired transition fails its domain and retains counted rows and pins. The correction adds two time reads per successful command (at admission and after target status); pending polls gain no time or register read; the host model still counts 14 PPU accesses for ON, five level reads per GPU admission and zero PMIC transactions per row request; the slow-acknowledgement case fails after 10,092 us.

conclusion: Deadline enforcement is implemented and host-tested. Physical evidence still required: one complete healthy GPU start, numerical operation, shutdown and reopen with owned memory and recovery intact (fresh firmware states, local idle/reset readbacks, PPU policy/status transitions, retained ownership on failure); a separate source-reviewed NPU OFF/ON procedure that excludes every shared-SRAM user; measured PPU completion latency and an intermediate status trace for both domains.
narrative:
Primary references (A733 board kernel revision 2ac08e8c7cdc28abbdc5c9a9dd812f887ae9c79f; the power-controller source, GPU source and both manuals match their sources.lock.json hashes; source adaptations preserve their license notices):
| Reference | Established behavior | Limit |
| pck600_domains.c lines 104-142 and 547-569 | Masked OFF/ON request, completion barrier, 10 ms polling bound, domain-specific delay words | Register status alone does not prove accelerator drain |
| pvr_power.c lines 94-111, 256-311 and 353-376; gpu-isolation.md | Firmware idle/OFF handshakes and local drain precede reset/gate teardown and platform power-off | Healthy firmware and owned memory only; failed-device recovery retains resources |
| vip_drv_device_platform.c lines 419-438 | NPU clock/reset initialization precedes runtime power-on; pm_runtime_put() is called before clock uninitialization | The call order does not establish when runtime PM completes OFF; GPU prerequisites cannot simply be copied |
| Arm PCK-600 TRM 101150_0005_01_en pages 34-35 and 40 | Configurable low-power interfaces coordinate quiescence, clock/reset/isolation control and the power-control state machine | A733 signal connections are implementation-specific; the TRM supplies no A733 software isolation register |
| A733 User Manual V1.00 section 2 printed page 4 | Shared SRAM 0x00074000-0x000f3fff requires NPU power while in use | Closing NPU command admission does not exclude other CPU or DMA SRAM users |

Concrete consumers: the GPU stop controller closes admission, obtains fresh firmware acknowledgements and independent power states, retires queues and checks BIF/MMU/cache/wrapper idle before reset readback; its platform controller then asserts external reset, closes local gates and requests domain 5 OFF, and the owner must acknowledge OFF before that platform releases resources; healthy reopening uses the ON row request with gates closed and reset asserted. NPU orderly CLOSE drains accepted work through its controller bounds, stops interrupts, closes local module and bus gates and asserts local engine resets; it retains domain 4, the SRAM reset state, PLL and leases. Full NPU OFF needs a concrete caller that proves no outstanding device work and no shared-SRAM users, plus a source-backed ordering between power completion and clock teardown; the thermal consumer supplies none, so the domain stays retained.

Deadline correction: before the correction the owner accepted a target status before testing whether its 10 ms transition deadline had expired, so a late OFF could unpin a rail. Now it rejects a status observation at or after the deadline and checks time again after a target read. A transition's deadline is the earlier of the service session deadline and 10 ms after the completed policy write; before programming delays or the policy the owner checks that the session remains open (this governs new commands and does not erase an adopted ON state or reclaim retained resources). The consumer's own earlier deadline remains its responsibility; the row API carries no per-consumer deadline.

hypothesis: Where the implementation of the owner and service differs from its original design.
conclusion: Each difference has a stated reason and is part of the present design.
narrative: No separate PPU clock lease: the owner reads R_CCU 0x1ac bit 0 at every admission and transition; every consumer already holds a stable PCK lease of the GPU resource manager before it requests its row, and the manager never disables a shared gate it enabled. A lease for the owner would need a client slot in every image that no session reserves. Bus-phase spin length: the service spins for the pending phase's expected duration from the provider (two bit times for START, repeated START and STOP, nine for a byte) timed from the provider's time of the phase-start write; with nine bit times for every phase a 400 kHz snapshot took three steps in the model, because a transaction has three conditions and four bytes. Fail functions do not notify: gpu_application_fail and the board's board_fail run from interrupt and fault paths where a FreeRTOS notification is not safe; an idle service holds no bus or lock and a pending transfer keeps it on one-tick steps, so it observes a revocation within one tick or at its next timed wake, at the latest the session deadline; park and stop requests from task context notify. Idle cap in the resident board image: the integrated OS image's watchdog requires the board PMIC service to report progress within 1 s, so that image's service blocks at most 500 ms when idle. The GPU row is registered by a733_gpu_platform_bind_pmic on the owner bound to the PMIC provider with the platform's owner and its DCDC4 consumer token; a733_power_domain_row_init is inline so targets that link the GPU platform without the owner still link; every GPU register write is a masked CCU update. Fault retention through the work query: a fault that a client latches while the service holds the I2C mutex sets the state word; the work query reports FAILED with RETAIN and the service polls once more so the provider marks its mutex retained. Mapping check at init: the native adapter checks the five windows once in its init before the scheduler. Verification budget: the 100 ms budget starts when the provider is READY after the settle time; a certain failed result is reaped and the token released; only the DCDC4 reading is kept for the GPU supply consumer. The NPU startup uses its domain-4 row and makes no PCK write; checks/power-domains-tree.py rejects direct NPU delay-row writes while a domain-4 row consumer exists. Merge-base branches: checks/rail-leases-cost-row.c and checks/power-domains-tree.py keep a branch for a tree with the DE_SYS provider for their --root measurement of the merge base. Verification only where a row exists, and a released token: the rail ledger has 32 holder slots for the 31 holders the images create, so the service releases the verification token after success and keeps it only after a failure; an image that registers no row, such as the integrated OS image, verifies nothing and makes no PMIC read at boot. Domain 1 and 4 OFF requests are refused at the request call. checks/a733-gpu-power.c keeps GPU-local cases with a stand-in; the real owner's trace for checks/a733-gpu-power-reference.py comes from checks/power-domains-pck.c.
